channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Euro-area industrial production fell further in August, with manufacturing down 0.5% from July against expected stagnation and output 1.1% below a year earlier, Eurostat data reported by Handelsblatt show.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that industrial production in the euro area declined further in August. According to Eurostat, manufacturing fell 0.5% from the previous month after economists had expected stagnation, and the July decline was revised to 0.3%, stronger than previously known. Year on year, output was 1.1% lower against an economists' forecast of a 0.1% fall. Handelsblatt adds that German companies increased production significantly in August, with industry, construction and energy utilities combined producing 2.0% more than in the previous month according to the Federal Statistical Office. The German figure covers industry, construction and energy together and is not directly comparable with the euro-area manufacturing figure. The row does not say which sectors drove the euro-area fall, whether the year-on-year figure is for manufacturing or for all industry, what the July figure was before revision, or how the German figure splits between industry and construction. It is a single source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures describe output in August, not orders or demand. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, industrial production is a broad indicator of activity at the manufacturers that buy industrial inputs, and a decline below forecasts points to weaker volumes at euro-area plants. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, volumes of industrial customers in the euro area are linked to sales of bonding, sealing and coating products, and the German increase covers a wider scope than the euro-area manufacturing figure, so the two are not a like-for-like contrast, which the source does not explain. Points that may be worth considering include the September production data, order and sentiment surveys, and whether the German rise is repeated.

Handelsblatt

item.title: China's customs data show September exports up 36.3% in dollar terms, with new energy passenger cars up 163.5%, and imports up 31% year on year, Lianhe Zaobao reports.
item.description:
Lianhe Zaobao reports General Administration of Customs information dated 14 October: in September imports rose 31% year on year and, in dollar terms, exports rose 36.3%; exports of new energy passenger cars rose 163.5%, automobile exports 53.2% and high-tech products 63.6%. The same outlet reports that the EU's trade deficit with China was a record USD 34.8 billion in September. MarketScreener gives the EU's goods trade deficit with China as EUR 360 billion in 2025 and about EUR 200 billion in the first six months of this year, with all EU countries in deficit and the deficit covering sectors from machinery to textiles, chemicals, plastics and cars. The Mainichi writes that China's industrial overcapacity is another major issue for the G20 finance ministers meeting in Bangkok on 15 October, noting that Chinese manufacturers export large volumes of goods, including steel, at lower prices. The row on China's data does not say which period the export percentages compare with, the level of exports or imports in dollars, which destinations drove the rise, or how much of it is price rather than volume. The EU deficit figures are in different currencies and periods and are not directly comparable. The China figures rest on one outlet's summary.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures give export value in dollars and say nothing about volumes or prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a large rise in Chinese exports of vehicles and other manufactured goods could increase the value, and possibly the volume, of competing products reaching other markets and adds to pressure for trade defence, which the EU is discussing for chemicals and machinery. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher Chinese vehicle and high-tech product exports could raise demand for bonding and sealing products at Chinese plants while increasing competition for European and other customers, and trade-defence responses could change input costs and market access. The row gives no figure for chemicals or materials exports. Points that may be worth considering include the next customs releases, whether chemical exports are reported separately, and how destination markets respond with trade measures.

Lianhe Zaobao, China customs data | Lianhe Zaobao, EU deficit | MarketScreener | The Mainichi

item.title: Ukraine appears to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries and, ABC reports, Zelenskyy says Kyiv is done supporting the US-announced energy ceasefire after Russian strikes on energy sites; the Guardian reports Washington's effort has collapsed.
item.description:
The Guardian reports that the White House's effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed after Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight against infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from President Trump; Moscow accused Ukraine of a first strike on a refinery in the Ryazan region since Trump declared the ceasefire. ABC reports that President Zelenskyy said Kyiv was "done" supporting the ceasefire, and that Trump blames attacks on energy infrastructure for raising diesel prices on global markets. Politico reports that Russian strikes hit 26 energy facilities and four oil and gas sites, leaving some 600,000 people without power, while Ukraine had not struck Russian energy sites since the announcement. Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that Zelenskyy also criticised a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence data and the throttling of the Starlink satellite internet service, and that the Kremlin said Kyiv was acting against US peace efforts. Anadolu Agency reports Zelenskyy as expressing support for the proposed energy ceasefire while saying Washington had earlier warned Kyiv that intelligence could be blocked if strikes on Russian energy sites did not stop. The accounts differ: the Guardian says neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to the ceasefire, while ABC says Trump announced that both had agreed. Business Recorder, citing the IEA, says the Middle East and Russia lost a combined 1.3 million barrels a day of diesel exports in September. The rows do not say which refineries were hit, beyond Moscow's accusation of a strike in the Ryazan region, or how much output was lost, whether US intelligence sharing was in fact reduced, or how much of Russia's diesel export loss is due to refinery strikes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a ceasefire that did not hold and renewed strikes on both sides; they give no measured change in Russian refinery output or exports after 15 October. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, strikes on refineries reduce the supply of diesel and other refined products, and strikes on power infrastructure reduce industrial activity in the affected areas. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, fuel prices and petrochemical feedstock costs feed into raw material, packaging and freight costs, and the sources do not say how far the strikes change them. Points that may be worth considering include reports of further refinery strikes, diesel and product prices, and whether the US continues to pursue an energy ceasefire.

The Guardian | ABC | Politico | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Anadolu Agency | Business Recorder

item.title: Von der Leyen lists chemicals and industrial machinery as priority industries for protection and suggests studying safeguards in the EU debate on Chinese imports, Commercial Times reports; the rows describe no adopted measure.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the EU leaders' summit on 15 October that chemicals and industrial machinery are priority industries for protection, suggested studying import quotas, tariffs and other safeguard measures, and presented a new trade tool proposed jointly by France and Germany that would quickly restrict companies' access to the single market when systemic market distortions or economic coercion are determined. Politico, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported that she was expected to say the Commission is looking at ways to protect the two sectors and that safeguards are the most effective tool currently available because they can be applied quickly and broadly. EUobserver quotes an EU diplomat saying the Commission "showed openness" to proposing safeguards, described as an emergency brake on imports that can cover entire sectors, and that there was "broad support" among member states. Handelsblatt describes two instruments called for by Paris and Berlin, one for rapid countermeasures in trade conflicts and one for trade diversification, which the Commission is to be able to activate without individual member states blocking them. Commercial Times speaks of one tool, Handelsblatt of two instruments. Lianhe Zaobao, citing informed sources cited by Bloomberg on 14 October, reported that Germany will ask the EU for safeguards in more industries, including chemicals, mechanical engineering and possibly pharmaceuticals. MarketScreener reports that draft summit conclusions indicate leaders will ask the Commission to continue the dialogue with Beijing, make full use of trade defence measures and add new trade instruments. The reporting does not say which chemical products would be covered, what quota or tariff levels are being considered, whether the summit conclusions name the two sectors, or when the Commission would propose measures, beyond Bloomberg's report that it will be urged to propose specific plans by the end of 2026. Most of the detail rests on anonymous sources and on previews, and only Commercial Times describes what was said at the summit.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reports name two sectors for possible protection and describe tools under discussion; the rows do not describe any adopted measure on chemical imports. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a safeguard limits the volume or raises the price of imports across a sector, and one covering chemicals could change both the cost of materials that European buyers source from China and the competition European producers face. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the effect would depend on whether the covered products are raw materials and intermediates the business buys or finished products it competes with, which the rows do not say. Points that may be worth considering include whether the summit conclusions name chemicals, which products the Commission lists when it proposes measures, and how a quota or tariff, if introduced, would apply to intermediates used in adhesives.

Commercial Times | Politico Europe | EUobserver | Handelsblatt | Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener

item.title: Hangzhou and Shenzhen issue rules prioritising existing and completed homes, with pre-sales of new projects tied to structural topping-out, Hangzhou implementing national rules of 28 August, Commercial Times and People's Daily report.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that Hangzhou's housing, planning and construction authorities and the Zhejiang financial regulator jointly issued trial implementation opinions on 15 October covering residential pre-sale management, existing-home sales, a lead bank system, financing support and land supply. The reform implements national residential sales regulations issued on 28 August by the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the Ministry of Natural Resources and the Financial Regulatory Administration, which require local governments to prioritise existing-home sales and reduce developers' financial pressure before completion through a lead bank system and development loans. Hangzhou distinguishes new and old projects by land acquisition and construction permit dates; if pre-sales are used for a new project, the main structure of a single building must be topped out, and all purchase funds go into a supervised account. People's Daily reports that Shenzhen introduced rules on 15 October to prioritise completed-home sales and tighten pre-sale requirements: for plots whose sale announcements were published after 28 August, pre-sales may start only once buildings reach full structural topping-out, and buyers may terminate deposit contracts if developers fail to deliver on schedule, with deposits refunded and liabilities borne by developers. The rows do not say how many projects or how much floor area the rules affect, how existing pre-sale projects are treated in Shenzhen, whether other cities are issuing similar rules, or what effect on completions or sales is expected. They cover two cities.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe changes to sales rules, not construction or sales figures. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, tying pre-sales to construction progress moves financing risk from buyers to developers and lenders, which could slow new starts while favouring projects close to completion. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the business's products are applied during construction and fit-out, so the timing of starts and completions at residential projects matters more for demand than headline home sales. The rows give no data on starts or completions. Points that may be worth considering include whether more cities publish implementing rules, how developers' land purchases and new starts respond, and whether lead-bank financing reaches projects.

Commercial Times | People's Daily Online

item.title: SIAM reports India's September passenger vehicle sales up 22% year on year to 454,574 units and up 28.3% in the first half of 2026-27; LiveMint reports Suzuki, Hyundai Motor Group and Stellantis have announced large investments.
item.description:
The Economic Times reports that the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) put September passenger vehicle sales at 454,574 units, up 22% year on year, with two-wheeler sales up 13.5% to 2.46 million and three-wheeler sales up 16% to 98,162. In the first half of the 2026-27 financial year passenger vehicle sales rose 28.3% to 2.64 million, commercial vehicle sales 23.8% to 564,255, two-wheeler sales 17.6% to 12.09 million and three-wheeler sales 26.3% to 501,879. LiveMint reports that at least three global automakers, Suzuki Motor, Hyundai Motor Group and Stellantis, have announced large investment commitments in India in recent months. Stellantis has committed an additional INR 40 billion over three years, bringing its cumulative India investment to INR 150 billion, to develop and launch 12 products including seven new nameplates and five refreshed models, the first in the second quarter of 2027. The rows do not say what the year-earlier base was, whether sales are registrations or wholesale dispatches, how much Suzuki and Hyundai plan to invest, or how much of the new capacity is for export. SIAM's figures come from one outlet's report.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures measure vehicle sales, and the investment rows describe commitments, not output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, vehicle sales growth of this size supports local assembly and component production, and new nameplates mean new platforms whose materials are specified in the coming years. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, India is a growing market for vehicle bonding, sealing and coating products if production follows sales, and new models are the point at which suppliers are qualified. The rows give no data on India's vehicle output or material sourcing. Points that may be worth considering include SIAM's next monthly figures, whether the growth rate holds against a higher base, and which suppliers the new nameplates use.

The Economic Times | LiveMint

item.title: Allianz Trade finds Chinese carmakers' EU market share rose from about 2% to almost 10% in recent years, with sales above 1 million units for the first time, and Fiev says carmakers are delisting European suppliers for Chinese ones.
item.description:
Anadolu Agency reports an Allianz Trade study showing that Chinese automakers' share of the EU market rose to almost 10% from 2% in recent years and that their sales across the continent exceeded 1 million units for the first time. In January–August the European car market grew 5% year on year, fully electric car sales rose 45% and fully electric cars reached 22% of new registrations, level with petrol cars. Over the past two years EU car exports to China declined while Chinese electric and hybrid car exports to the EU doubled to USD 14.2 billion in the first half of this year, with hybrid shipments alone up 206%, base period not given. Dünya Gazetesi, reporting overlapping figures, says Chinese brands account for 16% of all-electric and 26% of plug-in hybrid car sales in Europe. La Tribune reports that Fiev, a federation of vehicle equipment makers with activity in France, says European subcontractors face accelerating Chinese competition in parts and sub-assemblies, that manufacturers are delisting European equipment suppliers in favour of Chinese ones, and that China is accelerating parts exports; Europe produced 14.1 million light vehicles in 2025, 3.7 million fewer than in 2019. CNA reports that Chinese carmakers are pushing ahead with expansion plans at the Paris Auto Show despite the threat of tougher EU trade barriers. The rows do not give the year behind the 2% share, say how many suppliers have been delisted or in which parts, or separate sales built in Europe from imports.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures show market share and supplier pressure, not European production by plant. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, higher sales of Chinese brands in Europe, to the extent they are built in China, move part of vehicle production and parts sourcing away from European plants, and supplier delisting changes which plants buy materials. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, bonding, sealing and coating demand follows where cars and parts are built, so a shift of content to Chinese production could lower European demand and raise Chinese demand, while local-content rules under discussion in the EU could pull some of it back. The rows give no data on adhesives. Points that may be worth considering include the next registration and production data, whether European suppliers report lost contracts, and how local-content rules are defined.

Anadolu Agency | Dünya Gazetesi | La Tribune | CNA

item.title: A Forsa survey for FTI Andersch finds 15% of surveyed companies in Germany are relocating production facilities or planning to, rising to 31% among companies with sales above EUR 100 million, Handelsblatt reports.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports a survey by the opinion research institute Forsa for the restructuring consultancy FTI Andersch in which 15% of surveyed companies in Germany say they are relocating production facilities or planning to. Among companies with sales above EUR 100 million the share is 31%. Paul Niederstein, head of The Coatinc Company, does not expect investment conditions in Germany to improve in the medium term. The Handelsblatt headline refers to German industrial companies, while the summary speaks of companies in Germany. The row does not say how many companies were surveyed or when, which sectors the sample covers, whether relocation means moving abroad or any shift of capacity, which countries are named as destinations, or what share of output is affected. It is a single source, and the survey was commissioned by a restructuring consultancy.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The survey measures stated moves and plans of surveyed companies, not completed shifts in output or investment. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, production that leaves Germany takes its purchases of materials and processing with it, and the higher share among companies with sales above EUR 100 million suggests larger firms may be more ready to move than smaller ones. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German manufacturers in industries such as machinery, vehicles and building products buy bonding and coating products at their sites, so relocation by larger customers could change where demand arises more than how much of it there is, which the source does not quantify. Points that may be worth considering include the survey's sample and the destinations of relocated production, whether other German surveys show similar shares, and which customer industries are most affected.

Handelsblatt

item.title: Merz and Macron agree a car package that would relax the EU 2035 combustion-engine rules and reserve state purchase premiums and public contracts for European-made cars, Handelsblatt reports; Le Dauphiné calls it provisional.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President Emmanuel Macron agreed on a reform of European automotive policy. At Merz's insistence the 2035 combustion-engine rule is to be relaxed even more than the Commission had planned, and member states will no longer be obliged to promote electrification of large company car fleets through binding quotas. In return, state purchase premiums and public contracts will go only to cars manufactured in Europe, and a growing share of batteries and key vehicle components must come from European production. Süddeutsche Zeitung says EU fleet CO2 limits are to be relaxed by ten percentage points, from a 100% cut to 90% by 2035, and that France is pushing for the European-made condition to apply from 2028. Wirtschafts Woche reports that the compromise paper lets manufacturers cut average emissions by 90% from 2035 without compensating for the remaining 10%, and that France and six other EU countries had opposed a relaxation in June. Le Dauphiné, citing diplomatic sources, describes a provisional agreement under which European preference would cover production in the EU and close partners such as Great Britain or Norway. A later Handelsblatt report says, according to the German government, that a final agreement has yet to be reached; Wirtschafts Woche describes Germany's concession as favouring products of European origin in industrial funding, a wider wording than the car-specific terms above. The sources describe the relaxation differently: Süddeutsche Zeitung presents 90% as a cut from the 100% originally planned, while Handelsblatt says it goes beyond what the Commission had planned. The rows give the Commission's original plan only as Süddeutsche Zeitung's 100% and do not give its December proposal as a percentage, say how the battery and component share is defined, or say when the Council and Parliament will vote; the proposals do not enter into force without both.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The package is a provisional agreement between two governments on rules that are still before the Parliament and the Council, so the rows do not describe a law in force. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a softer 2035 CO2 rule keeps combustion-engine and hybrid cars in production for longer, while European-content conditions on subsidies, public contracts, batteries and components change which suppliers qualify. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, car makers and their suppliers are customers for bonding, sealing and coating products, so longer production of combustion and hybrid models alongside electric ones could keep demand for both sets of materials, and European-content rules could shift supplier choices toward production sites in the EU. The rows do not say how the content shares would be measured. Points that may be worth considering include whether the Council reaches a majority on the compromise, how the Parliament responds, and how the battery and component conditions are defined.

Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Wirtschafts Woche | Le Dauphiné Libéré | Handelsblatt, later report

item.title: The IEA agreed on 15 October to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel, the Globe and Mail reports; Handelsblatt says the remaining pledged stocks will bring about 100 million barrels to market, including 20 million of diesel.
item.description:
The Globe and Mail reports that on 15 October 2026 the International Energy Agency agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to a global market it describes as struggling with shortages and surging prices that are driving up inflation. Handelsblatt reports that the IEA wants to accelerate the release of emergency oil reserves, as Germany and the other G7 states demanded. According to Handelsblatt, the IEA had decided to release a record 400 million barrels of crude oil from strategic reserves, only around 330 million barrels have flowed so far, and the release of the remaining stocks pledged in March will now bring around 100 million barrels to the market, including 20 million barrels of diesel. Handelsblatt says this corresponds to the amount the G7 demanded. The Globe and Mail gives a record average retail diesel price in Canada of CAD 2.67 a litre this week, says diesel prices have eased from the all-time highs of more than USD 200 a barrel reached in September, and says global benchmarks remain nearly double the price of crude oil and their precrisis levels. Brent was at USD 105.81 on 15 October. The rows do not give a delivery schedule, the countries supplying the diesel, or whether the Globe and Mail's "more than 20 million barrels" is the same volume as Handelsblatt's 20 million. The two outlets use different wording, "agreed" and "wants to accelerate". Each volume rests on one outlet.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a decision to release diesel and a reported volume, not a measured change in prices or deliveries. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a release of more than 20 million barrels of diesel adds supply to a market the reports describe as short, which could ease diesel prices and the freight costs that follow them, depending on how fast the barrels reach buyers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, diesel prices feed into delivery costs for raw materials and finished goods, and crude and product prices feed into petrochemical raw material costs. The rows give no figure for the effect on prices. Points that may be worth considering include the delivery schedule, diesel and Brent prices after the release, and whether freight surcharges in supply contracts follow.

The Globe and Mail | Handelsblatt
